analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. prescription drug prices at the median price charged in eleven other developed countries.
analysis.headline: The bill was never acted on: introduced in June 2019 with one cosponsor, it was referred to six House committees and died there when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to set a yearly maximum price for every prescription drug, based on the median list price in countries like Japan, Germany, France, and Canada. Those caps would have applied to drugs bought through Medicare, Medicaid, the VA, TRICARE, and other federal health programs — and drug makers would have had to offer the same price to uninsured people and to anyone with private insurance. Companies that charged more would have faced a civil penalty worth five times the excess revenue, with the money going to NIH for drug research [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of people who take prescription drugs: seniors and people with disabilities on Medicare, families on Medicaid, veterans, military families, federal employees, and anyone uninsured or privately insured, since the cap extends to all buyers. Taxpayers also benefit because Medicare and Medicaid would pay less for the same drugs.

how_it_helps.text: HHS would set an annual reference price for each drug, using the median retail list price in eleven reference countries — Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Italy, Canada, Australia, Spain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Sweden — when pricing data exists in at least three of them [S3].
The cap applies to drugs under Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and Indian Health Service programs [S2][S3].
Drug makers must offer the reference price to uninsured individuals and people with private insurance, so the same low price follows patients outside the federal programs [S3].

Manufacturers that charge above the reference price face a civil penalty of five times the difference between what they received and what they would have received under the cap, and those penalties are transferred to the NIH for drug research and development [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose U.S. prices are generally the highest in the world and who would lose revenue from selling the same drugs at international price levels to the federal government, private insurers, and cash-paying patients.

drawbacks.text: Hard price caps tied to other countries' prices could reduce the revenue that funds research into new medicines, particularly for drugs sold mainly in the U.S., and the bill lets HHS set prices for drugs lacking three-country data based on its own judgment of value and development cost — a broad grant of discretion [S3].

Setting prices by administrative formula across every federal program and extending them into private markets is a major federal intervention that insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and drug distributors would have to implement, with transition and litigation costs the bill does not address [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: Americans pay roughly the highest drug prices in the developed world, and this bill would have pulled federal and private prices down to international levels, with penalties strong enough to make compliance the cheaper option. The main honest objection is that lower prices could mean somewhat less investment in new drugs over time. The bill's one-size cap on all drugs, including ones with thin international pricing data, was blunt, and the design questions it leaves unresolved (how HHS values a drug without comparable data) are serious. But the stakes for patients and taxpayers are large and the bill never received even a committee vote, so those design questions were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees on the day it was introduced, none of which ever took action on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch (D-VT) introduced the bill on June 26, 2019, joined by Rep. Francis Rooney (R-FL) as the sole cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].

The Speaker referred it to six committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Reform, and Natural Resources — splitting it across panels with jurisdiction over Medicare, Medicaid, the military health system, and more [S1][S5].

It went to subcommittees on Health and Military Personnel and others in the following weeks, but no committee reported it out and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who kept selling into Medicare, Medicaid, and private markets at prices far above what the same drugs fetch in other developed countries, and who faced no competing price cap that became law during this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 26, 2019, capping U.S. drug prices at international reference prices.

for.name: Rep. Francis Rooney
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House committees of jurisdiction (Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Reform, Natural Resources)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 26, 2019, but none held a markup or reported it out over the remaining 18 months of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Fought international reference pricing proposals of this kind throughout the 116th Congress through advertising and lobbying, contributing to the climate in which drug pricing bills stalled in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's two sponsors split across parties — a Democrat sponsoring, one of 197 House Republicans cosponsoring — and there were no recorded votes to show how the rest of the House would have lined up [S4].

industries.note: The bill caps their U.S. prices at the median of what they charge in eleven other countries and extends that price to all buyers, with penalties worth five times the excess revenue. Because U.S. prices are the industry's largest source of above-international profit, this is the single largest transfer the bill would have taken from an industry and given back to patients and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Private insurers would benefit from paying reference prices on their members' drugs, but the bill also dictates pricing in their markets and could squeeze rebate-negotiation models built around high list prices. The bill did not regulate their own pricing practices.
